pedagogy.summary: Ordering likelihoods asks children to compare several events and rank them least-to-most likely, including situations where outcomes are unequal (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections). Same-total comparisons are solvable by simple 'more/less' reasoning; the deeper demand — comparing across different totals — requires proportional reasoning, which the research shows develops slowly. Teaching should secure confident additive comparison and begin nudging children from absolute counts toward the proportion of favourable outcomes.
bestPractices: Build from same-total comparisons (which bag/section gives red the best chance when totals match) before introducing different totals
Make the proportional jump visible with a two-bag comparison where the bag with MORE red counters actually has a LOWER chance of red (e.g. 3 red of 4 vs 6 red of 12)
Have children physically order event cards along a least→most-likely line and defend each move
Press for reasons in terms of 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds', to shift attention from absolute number to proportion
Confront the 'it's random so you can't tell' response by sampling repeatedly and tallying, so order shows up in the long run
keyRepresentations: Two (or more) bags of counters compared side by side, part-whole visible
Spinners with sections of different sizes
Fraction/area strips linking proportion of red to chance of red
commonMisconceptions: Comparing by absolute count of favourable outcomes ('Bag B has 6 reds, Bag A only 3, so B is better') instead of proportion
The 'difference' strategy — comparing by the gap between the two colours (reds minus blues) rather than the fraction of the whole
Equiprobability bias — 'it's random, so every bag/colour is equally likely and you can't rank them'
Ranking by personal desire or by which outcome happened last, rather than by composition

learn.summary: Children aged 9–10 rank several chance events from least to most likely, including unequal outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections). Same-total comparisons yield to simple more/less reasoning; comparing across different totals demands proportional reasoning, which research shows develops slowly. Teaching should secure confident additive comparison, then nudge attention from absolute counts toward the proportion of favourable outcomes. The signature task sets up a case where the bag with MORE red counters has a LOWER chance of red (3 red of 4 vs 6 red of 12), and uses repeated sampling to let a count-based guess be publicly corrected by a long-run tally.

activities.title: Rank two bags, then test by sampling
feedback: If the child ranks Bag B higher because 'six reds beats three', run the sampling: over many draws Bag A will usually pull red more often (about three in every four draws against about one in two), and if a short run happens to mislead, pool more draws. Then point to all the counters in each bag, blues included, and ask 'out of ALL the counters, how much of each bag is red?' and shade three-quarters of A beside one-half of B.

If the child says 'it's random, you can't tell which is better', sample many draws from each bag and tally; the long-run difference is visible even though each single draw is unpredictable — this separates 'random' from 'equally likely'.

When the child re-ranks Bag A to the top and justifies with the share of the whole, confirm that this share is what the growing tally gets close to: over many draws the fraction of reds moves towards the share, but it rarely matches it exactly.

On the 60-red/40-blue extension, if the child now favours Bag B because the numbers are big, compare shares directly: three-fifths is still less than three-quarters, so bigger raw counts do not by themselves make a better chance.
activities.rationale: Comparing across different totals requires proportional reasoning, and children frequently fall back on raw frequency; making the count-based ordering publicly wrong and then visible as a share targets that shift. Repeated sampling addresses the belief that a random situation cannot be ranked. An editable-bag-plus-sampler arrangement is one concrete way to let a wrong ranking be tested; a physical version with real bags, replacing each counter before the next draw, and tally marks works the same way.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.

The equiprobability bias — assuming outcomes are all equally likely / that a random situation cannot be ranked — is documented in children as young as 10 (Pratt) as a first response to chance situations.
learnerActions: Look at Bag A (3 red, 1 blue) and Bag B (6 red, 6 blue), both fully visible, and rank which gives the better chance of pulling red before any draws.
State a reason for the ranking out loud.

Draw many times from each bag (e.g. 50 draws each), noting each drawn counter's colour and returning it to the bag before the next draw so the proportion stays fixed, and tally how often red comes up, comparing the two tallies.
Revise the ranking if the tally contradicts the first guess, and say why — in terms of how big a share of each bag is red, not how many reds.
Look at a shaded red-fraction strip beside each tally (three-quarters of A, one-half of B) and connect the share to the observed long-run frequency.

As an extension, suppose Bag B instead held 60 red and 40 blue: check whether these bigger numbers change the ranking (60 of 100 is three-fifths, higher than one-half but still below Bag A's three-quarters, so Bag A is still the better bet).
activities.intendedInsight: A better chance of red depends on the proportion of red in the whole bag (three-quarters beats one-half), not on the raw number of red counters — so a bag with more reds can still be the worse bet.

activities.title: Order four or more events on a least→most-likely line
feedback: If the child orders by raw count of reds, swap in a card with more reds but a smaller share and ask them to predict and then check by sampling.
If the child ranks by personal preference or by which outcome happened last, redirect to the composition: 'how many out of the whole is red here?'
Press for 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds' on every placement.
activities.rationale: Physically ordering and defending each move makes the ranking an explicit, revisable claim rather than a one-off guess, and building from same-total to different-total comparisons sequences the additive before the proportional demand. Socratic challenge ('what if I doubled the blues?') surfaces the reasoning; the proportional point may land more firmly when the child can also manipulate and sample, so pair argument with testing where possible.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.
Likelihood is described with a graded word-scale and 'even chance' applies only when outcomes genuinely match in number, motivating comparison of bags/spinners by composition.
learnerActions: Physically place four or more event cards along a 'least likely → most likely' rail (e.g. different bags or spinners with varying red fractions).
Defend each placement, and each time a card is moved, say why it should sit higher or lower.
Respond to a challenge such as 'why is that one higher? what if I doubled the blues?' by giving a reason in terms of the share of the whole, not just the number of reds.
Start with cards that share the same total (so simple more/less reasoning works) before mixing in cards with different totals.
activities.intendedInsight: Events can be placed in a consistent order of likelihood by comparing the proportion of favourable outcomes; same-total cases need only more/less, but different-total cases need the share of the whole.

activities.title: Spinner prediction: does section size matter?
feedback: If the child predicts roughly equal because 'it could land on either', spin and tally: red near 15 vs blue near 5 confronts the prediction and forces attention to section size.
Use the follow-up 'could the less-likely colour still come up next spin?' to separate 'more likely in the long run' from 'certain on a single trial'.
Reserve 'even chance' for cases where the outcomes genuinely match in number, so the child does not over-apply it to unequal spinners.
activities.rationale: Predict-then-test on an unequal spinner directly targets equiprobability bias by letting a prediction of 'about the same' be contradicted by the tally, while the single-trial follow-up guards against treating 'more likely' as 'certain'. The graded likelihood word-scale and the restriction of 'even chance' to matched outcomes motivate comparing by composition.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming outcomes are all equally likely / that a random situation cannot be ranked — is documented in children as young as 10 (Pratt) as a first response to chance situations.
Likelihood is described with a graded word-scale and 'even chance' applies only when outcomes genuinely match in number, motivating comparison of bags/spinners by composition.
learnerActions: Look at a spinner where red fills three-quarters and blue one-quarter, alongside a fair coin.
Before spinning, predict: over 20 spins, will red and blue come up about the same number of times, or will one come up much more — and state a reason.
Spin 20 times and tally red versus blue (expect red near 15, blue near 5).
Compare the tally to the prediction and explain what the size of each section did to the outcome.
Consider follow-ups: could the less-likely colour still come up on the very next spin? What does 'more likely' actually mean here?
activities.intendedInsight: When outcomes are not equally sized, 'it could land on either' does not make them equally likely — the size (proportion) of each section governs the long-run frequency, and a more-likely outcome can still fail on a single trial.

activities.title: The 'difference' trap: 20 red vs 18 blue
feedback: If the child says the two bags are equally good because each has 2 more reds than blues, show that 3 of 4 is three-quarters while 20 of 38 is barely above one-half: equal gaps, very different chances — this forces the comparison onto the fraction of the whole.
If the child still leans on the gap, convert each bag to 'how many out of the whole is red' and compare those shares directly.
Confirm success when the child abandons the gap and ranks by the share of red in each bag.
activities.rationale: The 'difference' strategy is a documented additive fallback; pairing two bags with an identical gap but very different proportions exposes it without relying on the child already trusting the proportional rule. This is a targeted correction to use once absolute-count errors are being addressed.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.
learnerActions: Compare a bag of 20 red and 18 blue with a clearly lopsided bag of 3 red and 1 blue, and decide which gives the better chance of red. Notice that BOTH bags have the same gap: 2 more reds than blues.
Explain the reasoning, noticing whether it rests on the gap between the colours (reds minus blues) or on the share of the whole.
Work out what share of each bag is red (close to one-half for 20 of 38, three-quarters for 3 of 4) and use that to place both in order.
Check the conclusion by sampling (with each counter returned before the next draw) if a count-based or difference-based answer is given.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing by the gap between the two colours (reds minus blues) can mislead: 20 red and 18 blue and 3 red and 1 blue both have a gap of 2, yet 20 of 38 is almost an even chance while 3 of 4 is three-quarters — so the fraction of the whole, not the surplus of reds, decides likelihood.

constraints: Build from same-total comparisons (which bag/section gives red the best chance when totals match) before introducing different totals.

A pre-ordered likelihood line with tap-to-reveal reasons ('X out of Y, so …') is a useful worked reference, but as a fixed display it does not itself let the child test a wrong ranking or carry out the proportional correction; use it to model good ordering, not as the sole activity.

Multiple-choice or drag-to-order response formats can carry the key discriminator (e.g. 3-of-4 vs 6-of-12 with distractors 'B, it has more reds' and 'the same, it's random') and can be used during teaching as well as for checking; recognition-format responses alone do not require the child to construct and defend a ranking, so pair them with spoken or written justification.

Repeated sampling is central to confronting the 'it's random, you can't tell' response: a single draw is unpredictable, but tallying many draws reveals the long-run order. Sample with replacement (return each counter) so the stated proportions stay fixed across many draws.
Always press for reasons in terms of 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds'.
Reserve 'even chance' for situations where the outcomes genuinely match in number.
When observing spinners or bags, inspect the actual drawn/spun outcomes and tallies; a short run may vary from the expected proportion, so pool more draws if a run happens to mislead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled ranking likelihoods a non-spatial task where '3D adds no leverage'; this catalog-fit judgement is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped rather than asserted. No universal claim about any medium is made here.

The suggestion that manipulation/sampling makes the proportional insight land more firmly than argument alone is a comparative-efficacy framing not established by the cited literature; it is stated with 'may' as a design suggestion only.

The sampling activities assume drawing with replacement; with only 4 and 12 counters, the child must return each drawn counter before the next draw for many-draw tallies to reflect the fixed proportion.

Sampling 50 or 20 draws yields outcomes near the expected proportions (e.g. red near 15 of 20 for a three-quarter spinner) but will vary run to run; frame these as approximate long-run tendencies, and if a short run happens to mislead, pool more draws or combine results across the group.

The worked numbers are internally consistent: 3 of 4 = three-quarters > 6 of 12 = one-half, so Bag A is correctly the better chance of red; 20 of 38 for the 20-red/18-blue bag is just above one-half, consistent with 'nearly even'; and 60 of 100 = three-fifths is below three-quarters, so Bag A stays ahead in the extension.
The 'difference' trap pairs two bags with an identical gap of 2 (20/18 and 3/1) so that a reds-minus-blues strategist is genuinely misled, matching the original diagnostic intent.

assess.poeTask: Show a spinner divided so that red fills three-quarters and blue one-quarter, alongside a fair coin. Ask: 'Over 20 spins, will red and blue come up about the same number of times, or will one come up much more — and why?' Have the child state a prediction AND a reason before spinning. A child who thinks 'it could land on either, so about the same' predicts roughly equal; spinning 20 times and tallying (red near 15, blue near 5) confronts that prediction and forces attention to the size of each section.
probeDeeper: What if I now told you Bag B had 60 red and 40 blue — would that change your answer? Why?
Cover up the blue counters. Just from the reds, can you tell which bag is better? What else do you need to know?
Suppose a third bag had 20 red and 18 blue — where would it go in the order, and why?
You said one is 'more likely'. Could the less-likely bag still give a red on the very next pull? So what does 'more likely' actually mean here?
assess.correctAnswer: Bag A. Even though Bag B contains more red counters (6 versus 3), three of the four counters in Bag A are red — three-quarters — while only six of the twelve in Bag B are red — one half. Bag A has the higher proportion of red, so a better chance.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares by absolute count of favourable outcomes — 'Bag B, it has more red counters (6 beats 3)'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Direct attention to the whole: cover the blues and ask 'out of ALL the counters, how much of each bag is red?'; shade three-quarters of A and one-half of B side by side
errorPatterns.distractor: Bag B, because it has more red counters — 6 reds, and Bag A only has 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks Bag B and reasons from the raw number of reds, ignoring how many counters there are altogether

errorPatterns.pattern: Equiprobability bias — 'it's the same, pulling a counter is random so you can't say which bag is better'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sample many draws from each bag and tally; the long-run difference is visible even though each single draw is unpredictable, separating 'random' from 'equally likely'
errorPatterns.distractor: It's the same — pulling a counter is random, so you can't say which bag is better.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says both bags are equally good and appeals to randomness/luck rather than composition

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Difference' strategy — compares by the gap between the colours (reds minus blues) rather than the proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Offer the 20-red/18-blue counterexample: a difference of 2 but almost an even chance; force the comparison onto the fraction of the whole, not the gap
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reason cites the surplus of reds over blues ('A has 2 more reds than blues; B has none more'); gives the wrong answer when shown a bag like 20 red / 18 blue (gap of 2 but nearly even)

responseLevels.gap: Cannot rank beyond guessing or says 'it's random, you can't tell'; ordering ignores composition entirely
responseLevels.full: Ranks by the proportion of favourable outcomes, picks Bag A and justifies with three-quarters vs one-half, and keeps the ranking correct when totals are changed; recognises a more-likely event can still fail on a single trial
responseLevels.partial: Ranks correctly when totals are equal or by counting favourable outcomes, but picks the larger-count bag when proportion and count diverge, or reasons from the red-minus-blue difference — lists the numbers without converting to a share of the whole

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two bags of counters, both visible. Bag A: 3 red and 1 blue. Bag B: 6 red and 6 blue. Ask: 'Which bag gives you a better chance of pulling out a red — and why?' Take their answer, then ask them to explain their reason fully (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A proportional reasoner picks Bag A and justifies with the fraction of red in each bag; a child using absolute counts picks Bag B because it has more red counters; an equiprobability-biased child says 'the same, it's random'. The Tier-2 reason exposes which, and only the proportional reason survives when the totals are then changed.
